content: This report does not address the off-label use of products or investigational products, except for the discussion of off-label use of the zoster vaccine in individuals with a history of herpes zoster. The content of this report originates from the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, under the direction of Anne Schuchat, MD. Infection with the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes two distinct diseases: varicella (chickenpox) and herpes zoster (shingles). Universal varicella vaccination is recommended for all individuals older than 12 months who lack evidence of immunity. The introduction of the varicella vaccine has significantly reduced the incidence of chickenpox among children. Herpes zoster, or shingles, is a localized and often painful cutaneous eruption that occurs most frequently in older adults. Approximately one million new cases of zoster are reported annually in the United States, with about one in three individuals developing zoster during their lifetime. A common complication of zoster is postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), a chronic pain condition that can persist for months or even years. The zoster vaccine was licensed in the United States for individuals aged 60 years and older. This report provides recommendations for the use of the zoster vaccine to prevent zoster and its complications. The vaccine was developed based on a phase 3 clinical trial, with results published in June 2005 and presented at the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) meeting later that month. In September 2005, the ACIP expanded its measles-mumps-rubella and varicella workgroup to include experts in adult medicine and zoster. This group reviewed data on zoster and the investigational vaccine, holding 19 conference calls to evaluate scientific evidence on the epidemiology, natural history, safety, immunogenicity, efficacy, and logistics of the zoster vaccine. They also reviewed economic analyses of zoster prevention. The workgroup developed and discussed recommendations for zoster prevention, incorporating expert opinions when scientific evidence was lacking. Presentations on zoster and the vaccine were made during ACIP meetings in 2005 and 2006. Following the vaccine's licensure in May 2006, recommendation options were presented to ACIP in June 2006, with final recommendations presented in October 2006. Modifications were made to the proposed recommendations during review by the CDC and external partners to ensure clarity and accuracy. As new information on zoster epidemiology and prevention becomes available, ACIP will review and update recommendations as needed. Biology of Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) VZV is an exclusively human pathogen that infects approximately 98% of the adult population in the United States. Primary infection typically occurs during childhood, causing varicella (chickenpox). During the viremic phase, cell-associated VZV spreads to epidermal cells, resulting in the characteristic varicella rash. The virus then enters sensory nerves at mucocutaneous sites and travels retrogradely to the sensory dorsal root ganglia near the spinal cord, where it establishes permanent latency in neuronal cell bodies. Latent VZV is present in approximately 1%-7% of sensory ganglion neurons, with fewer than 10 genomic copies per infected cell. The magnitude of viremia, the number of skin lesions, and the viral burden during primary infection may influence the establishment of latency. Like other herpesviruses, VZV is noninfectious in its latent form but can reactivate later to produce intact virions in sensory neurons. These virions migrate to the skin via axons, spread cell-to-cell, and penetrate the epidermis, causing shingles. The triggers for VZV reactivation are not fully understood but likely involve multiple factors. Components of cell-mediated immunity (CMI) play a critical role in controlling zoster by preventing reactivation or the full clinical expression of reactivated VZV. CMI responses are well-maintained in immunocompetent individuals during childhood and early adulthood, with periodic immunologic boosting from subclinical reactivation or exposure to circulating VZV. Although nearly all adults are infected with VZV, specific immunologic parameters that predict who will develop zoster have not been identified. Anti-VZV antibody levels are not thought to play a role in zoster prevention. Parameters associated with protection include anamnestic boosting of anti-VZV antibodies in response to vaccination and the presence of memory CD4 T cells, as measured by proliferation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) or interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) release in response to VZV antigens. Clinical Features of Zoster and Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN) The clinical course of acute zoster varies and is generally less severe in children and younger adults. Zoster typically begins with a prodrome, which may include headache, photophobia, malaise, and occasionally fever. Abnormal skin sensations and pain of varying severity are the most common symptoms, often preceding the rash by days to weeks. Pain is described as aching, burning, stabbing, or shock-like, and altered sensitivity to touch, pain from trivial stimuli, and intense itching are frequently reported. The zoster rash is usually unilateral and confined to one or two adjacent dermatomes. It begins as an erythematous maculopapular rash that progresses to clusters of clear vesicles containing high concentrations of VZV. The vesicles evolve through pustular, ulcerative, and crusting stages, with the rash typically resolving within 7-10 days and complete healing within 2-4 weeks. However, pigmentation changes and scarring may be permanent. A common and potentially debilitating consequence of zoster is PHN, characterized by persistent pain after the rash resolves. Pathologic findings in PHN include axonal and neuronal degeneration, atrophy of the spinal cord dorsal horn, scarring of the dorsal root ganglion, and loss of epidermal innervation. Some experts believe ongoing viral replication may contribute to neuronal damage. The pain of PHN can range from mild to excruciating, constant or intermittent, and may be triggered by trivial stimuli. It can disrupt sleep, mood, work, and daily activities, adversely affecting quality of life and leading to social withdrawal and depression. Transmission of Zoster Zoster lesions contain high concentrations of VZV, which can be transmitted via airborne routes and cause primary varicella in susceptible individuals. Localized zoster is contagious only after the rash erupts and until the lesions crust. Zoster is less contagious than varicella, with transmission risk reduced if lesions are covered. Epidemiology and Risk Factors Zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV, with prior VZV infection being a necessary precondition. Age is the most significant risk factor, with incidence increasing substantially after age 50. Approximately 50% of individuals who live to age 85 will experience zoster. Immunosenescence and waning immunity contribute to the increased risk with age. Immunocompromised individuals, including those with hematologic malignancies or undergoing stem cell transplantation, are at significantly higher risk for zoster and its complications.
